passages.happening:
The book opens with a death and a command. “Now after the death of His servant Moses, the LORD spoke to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ assistant” (verse 1).

God's first words are blunt. “Moses My servant is dead. Now therefore arise, you and all these people, and cross over the Jordan into the land that I am giving to the children of Israel” (verse 2). He describes the land, from the wilderness in the south to Lebanon in the north, and from the Euphrates River to the Great Sea, which is the Mediterranean (verse 4).

Then come the promises. “No one shall stand against you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so will I be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you” (verse 5).

Three times God tells Joshua to be strong and courageous (verses 6, 7 and 9). The middle time he says what the courage is for: “Be careful to observe all the law that My servant Moses commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right or to the left” (verse 7). “This Book of the Law must not depart from your mouth; meditate on it day and night” (verse 8).

The speech ends where it began, with God's presence: “Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Israel had never known a day without Moses. He had led the people out of Egypt, stood between them and God at Sinai, and carried them for forty years. Now he is dead, and the river is still in front of them. The first thing God says is the thing everyone is thinking.

Joshua is called Moses' assistant. He had served beside Moses since he was young, and Moses had already laid hands on him and appointed him before the people (Numbers 27:18-23). God does not give him a new plan. He gives him the same promise in a new mouth: ‘just as I promised to Moses’ (verse 3).

The verbs matter. The land is something God ‘is giving’ and ‘has given’. Israel will have to walk into it and fight for it, but the book wants its readers to see the land as a gift before they see a single battle.

The land described in verse 4 is very wide. Israel never held all of it in Joshua's day. It came closest under David and Solomon, long afterward.

A new reader might expect a general to be told about weapons and plans. Joshua is told to read. The Book of the Law is the teaching Moses wrote down and left with the priests. In Deuteronomy a future king was told to keep a copy and read it all his life (Deuteronomy 17:18-19). Joshua is treated like that king. His success depends on staying close to what God has said.

The word ‘meditate’ does not mean sitting in silence with an empty mind. The Hebrew word means to murmur or mutter. It is used elsewhere for a lion growling over its food and a dove moaning. To meditate on the law was to say it over under the breath, again and again, until it was part of the speaker. That is why the book must not leave Joshua's mouth.

The word ‘prosper’ needs care. The Hebrew behind it includes acting wisely and with insight, and not only coming out ahead. The promise was made to Joshua for the task God gave him. It is not a rule that anyone who reads the Bible will grow rich or win.

And the command to be brave rests on a reason. Joshua is not told to find courage in himself. He is told, ‘the LORD your God is with you’.
passages.later:
Moses had said the same words to Joshua in front of all Israel: “The LORD Himself goes before you; He will be with you. He will never leave you nor forsake you” (Deuteronomy 31:8).

The first psalm describes the kind of person verse 8 has in view: “But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2).

The letter to the Hebrews takes the promise of verse 5 and gives it to every believer: “for God has said: ‘Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.’” (Hebrews 13:5). And the last words of Jesus in Matthew's Gospel are a promise of the same kind: “And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).
passages.asks: God began with the loss: ‘Moses My servant is dead.’ Ask what has ended for you, a person, a season or a way of doing things, that you have not yet said plainly. Then ask what God is asking you to do next, and whether you are looking for the courage in yourself or in the one who says he will be with you. Ask what place his words have in your mouth during an ordinary day.

passages.t: Three days, and a promise kept by the eastern tribes
passages.happening:
Joshua acts at once. He tells the officers to go through the camp with an order: ‘Prepare your provisions, for within three days you will cross the Jordan’ (verse 11).

Then he turns to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh. These tribes had already been given land east of the Jordan. Joshua reminds them of what Moses told them: ‘The LORD your God will give you rest, and He will give you this land’ (verse 13). Their wives, children and herds may stay. But their fighting men must cross with the others and help them, ‘until the LORD gives them rest as He has done for you’ (verse 15). Then they may go home.

They answer without holding back. “Everything you have commanded us we will do, and everywhere you send us we will go. Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. And may the LORD your God be with you, as He was with Moses” (verses 16-17).

They even add their own warning for anyone who rebels, and they close with the words God had used: ‘Above all, be strong and courageous’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The officers were the men who kept order and passed on commands in the camp. Their task is simple: tell every family to get food ready. The manna was still falling, but people going to war in a new country would need supplies.

The eastern tribes are the first test of Joshua's leadership. After Israel defeated the kings Sihon and Og, these tribes asked Moses for the land east of the river, because it was good for their herds. Moses agreed on one condition. Their soldiers had to cross with everyone else and fight until the others had land too (Numbers 32:20-22). Now Moses is gone, and they are already home. They could have said that the promise died with him. They do not.

The word ‘rest’ appears here for the first time in the book. It means a settled home and an end of war. The eastern tribes already have it. They are asked to leave it for a while so that their brothers can have it too. The book will come back to this word again and again.

Their pledge sounds like the oath of loyalty that people in the ancient world swore to a ruler, with death named as the price of rebellion. It belongs to a people at war under a commander. It is not a pattern for how any leader today may treat those who disagree.

One phrase in their answer is a prayer and also a condition: ‘may the LORD your God be with you, as He was with Moses’. They will follow Joshua as a man God is with. And the chapter ends with the people saying back to Joshua the very words God had said to him. The leader who has to give courage to everyone else is given it by them.
passages.later:
The book keeps its word about these tribes. Many chapters later Joshua sends them home with thanks: ‘You have done all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you’ (Joshua 22:2).

The promise of rest runs on through the Bible. Hebrews says that the rest Joshua gave was not the last: “For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day” (Hebrews 4:8). And Jesus says, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).
passages.asks: The eastern tribes already had what they wanted, and they crossed the river anyway. Ask who is still waiting for something you already have: a home, steady work, a place in the church, peace. Ask what it would cost you to help them reach it. And notice who said ‘be strong and courageous’ to Joshua at the end. Ask who needs to hear it from you.
